newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson awarded custody of his two children.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson awarded custody of his two children.

text.p: O.J. Simpson was awarded full custody of his two youngest children on Friday, more than 2-1/2 years after their mother was killed and their American football star father was charged with her murder.
Orange County Judge Nancy Wieben Stock ruled that Sydney, 11, and Justin, 8, who have lived with their maternal grandparents since just after their mother's death, should be returned to their father.

Simpson, who was acquitted in October 1995 in the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman, issued a statement, saying, "We are all so very grateful to have the children home again where they want to be."

But Natasha Roit, the Browns' attorney, denounced the judge's decision, saying living with Simpson would expose the children to "substantial risk" with a man who had beaten their mother and "has continued to deny that he is a batterer."
Louis and Judith Brown, who were granted visitation rights, said they received the news with "great sadness and concern."
"I think what happened here was devastating," a tearful Denise Brown, Nicole Brown Simpson's older sister, said on CNN's "Larry King Live."

The judge's ruling capped a bitter custody fight between the Browns and Simpson, but the Hall of Fame running back's legal troubles are far from over -- he is still on trial in civil court, facing a wrongful-death lawsuit brought by the victims' families.
During the custody battle, the Browns' attorneys contended Simpson was an unfit parent, citing allegations of domestic violence.

But Simpson's attorneys argued he had the right to full custody as the biological father. Simpson also expressed concern that living with the Browns, who are white, the children were not being properly instructed in their black heritage.

The judge noted that the children showed no signs of "fear or intimidation around their father" and ruled that the Browns failed to provide convincing evidence that living with Simpson would be harmful.

Simpson signed temporary guardianship of the children over to the Browns after his arrest on June 17, 1994, and the children have lived with them for 2-1/2 years in the Orange County coastal community of Dana Point.
After his release last year, Simpson, who had weekend visits with his children, asked to get them back. The Browns refused and sought legal custody.
Under the judge's 11-page ruling, Roit said, the children can spend the upcoming holidays with Simpson, but they cannot be moved permanently out of the Browns' home before Jan. 10.
Stock scheduled a hearing on that date on the Browns' request to stay the children's transfer and the termination of the guardianship while they decide whether to appeal the decision.
The children's whereabouts were not immediately known.
Simpson pleaded for "the media and the public to allow my children their privacy and to live in as normal an environment as possible."

But the Browns left no doubt about their concern for the safety of their grandchildren, saying they had fought to prevent them from being exposed "to the risks and detriment of domestic violence which plagued their past and, if returned to Mr. Simpson, would be likely to affect their future."
Testifying last month at his civil trial, Simpson steadfastly denied ever having beaten or abused his ex-wife despite a photograph of her bruised, swollen face that was shown to the jury.
Legal experts said California law favoured Simpson, as the natural parent, and even the attorney appointed to represent the children reportedly recommended they be turned over to him.
